sections.title: Detailed Brief Overview
rows: Constitutional guarantees of civil liberties (**Fundamental Rights**) and civic obligations (**Fundamental Duties**).
Fundamental Rights enforced on **January 26, 1950**; Fundamental Duties added on **January 3, 1976**.
Enshrined in **Part III (Articles 12-35)** and **Part IV-A (Article 51A)** of the **Constitution of India**.
Drafted by the **Constituent Assembly** (Fundamental Rights Sub-committee headed by **J.B. Kripalani**); Duties added via **Swaran Singh Committee**.
Essential for intellectual, moral, and spiritual development of citizens; ensures balance between individual liberty and social control.
Justiciable rights (**Article 32**), non-justiciable duties, borrow-inspired from **USA** (Rights) and **USSR** (Duties).
High-yielding static polity section covering article numbers, amendments, writs, and landmark cases.
**Article 32** called 'Heart and Soul of the Constitution' by **Dr. B.R. Ambedkar**; Originally 10 duties, now **11 duties**.

items.title: Origin and Borrowed Sources
items.content:
• **Fundamental Rights** borrowed from the **Constitution of USA** (Bill of Rights).
• Contained in **Part III** of the Constitution, spanning **Articles 12 to 35**.
• Described as the **Magna Carta of India** due to its comprehensive nature.
• **Fundamental Duties** borrowed from the erstwhile **USSR** (now Russia).
• Added to **Part IV-A** via the **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976**.
• **Mnemonic for Sources:** **'U S'** (Rights = **U**SA, Duties = **S**oviet Union/USSR).

items.title: Classification of Fundamental Rights
items.content:
• **Right to Equality** (**Articles 14-18**): Ensures equality before law and prohibition of discrimination.
• **Right to Freedom** (**Articles 19-22**): Guarantees six democratic freedoms and protection of life/liberty.
• **Right against Exploitation** (**Articles 23-24**): Prohibits human trafficking, forced labor, and child labor.
• **Right to Freedom of Religion** (**Articles 25-28**): Guarantees freedom of conscience and free profession, practice, and propagation of religion.
• **Cultural and Educational Rights** (**Articles 29-30**): Protects interests of minorities and their right to establish educational institutions.
• **Right to Constitutional Remedies** (**Article 32**): Empowers citizens to move Supreme Court for enforcement.
• **Mnemonic for Rights:** **'E F E R C R'** (**E**quality, **F**reedom, **E**xploitation-free, **R**eligion, **C**ultural, **R**emedies).

items.title: Six Freedoms under Article 19
items.content:
• Freedom of **Speech and Expression** (**Article 19(1)(a)**).
• Freedom of **Assembly** peacefully and without arms (**Article 19(1)(b)**).
• Freedom to form **Associations or Unions or Cooperative Societies** (**Article 19(1)(c)**).
• Freedom of **Movement** freely throughout the territory of India (**Article 19(1)(d)**).
• Freedom of **Residence** and settlement in any part of India (**Article 19(1)(e)**).
• Freedom of **Profession, Occupation, Trade or Business** (**Article 19(1)(g)**).
• **Mnemonic for Article 19:** **'S A A M R P'** (**S**peech, **A**ssembly, **A**ssociation, **M**ovement, **R**esidence, **P**rofession).

items.title: Writs under Article 32 and 226
items.content:
• **Habeas Corpus:** To have the body of; protects against illegal detention.
• **Mandamus:** We command; orders a public official to perform a duty.
• **Prohibition:** To forbid; issued by higher court to lower court to stop excess jurisdiction.
• **Certiorari:** To be certified; issued to quash an order of a lower court.
• **Quo-Warranto:** By what authority; prevents illegal usurpation of a public office.
• **Mnemonic for Writs:** **'H M P C Q'** (**H**abeas, **M**andamus, **P**rohibition, **C**ertiorari, **Q**uo-Warranto).

items.title: Evolution of Fundamental Duties
items.content:
• Recommended by the **Swaran Singh Committee** in **1976**.
• Added via **42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976** with **10 duties** under **Article 51A**.
• **11th Fundamental Duty** added by the **86th Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002**.
• Relates to providing opportunities for education to child between age **6 and 14 years**.
• **Non-justiciable** in nature (cannot be enforced by courts directly).
• **Mnemonic for Duties Amendment:** **42** (**4 + 2 = 6**, Swaran Singh era) and **86** (Education duty).

items.definition: Remember the categories by splitting: **14-18** (Equality), **19-22** (Freedom), **23-24** (Exploitation), **25-28** (Religion), **29-30** (Culture/Education), **32** (Remedies). Total 6 categories.

Remember that **Article 17** (Untouchability), **Article 18** (Titles), **Article 24** (Child Labour), and **Article 20-21** (Emergency protections) have strict limits, while **Article 19** freedoms are subject to reasonable restrictions.
Memorize writs using **HEMA** (**H**abeas Corpus, **M**andamus) and **PRO QUO** (**Pro**hibition, **C**ertiorari, **Quo**-Warranto).
Property was Article **31** and **19(1)(f)**. It was shifted to Article **300A** in Part **XII** by the **44th** Amendment in **1978**.
Started with **10** (42nd Amendment, 1976), added **1** more (86th Amendment, 2002), making a total of **11** duties under Article **51A**.
Remember **B.R. Ambedkar** called **Article 32** the 'Heart and Soul' because without a remedy, a right is meaningless.
Students confuse Fundamental Rights with Fundamental Duties. **Fundamental Rights** are justiciable (can go to court), whereas **Fundamental Duties** are non-justiciable.
Many think Right to Property is still a Fundamental Right. It is now a constitutional/legal right under **Article 300A**, not Part III.
Confusing **Article 21** (Right to Life) with **Article 21A** (Right to Education added by 86th Amendment).
Students often think Fundamental Duties were part of the original 1950 Constitution. They were added in **1976** by the **42nd Amendment**.
Thinking all Fundamental Rights are suspended during National Emergency. **Articles 20 and 21** can **NEVER** be suspended.
Forgetting that both Supreme Court (**Article 32**) and High Courts (**Article 226**) can issue writs, but High Court's writ jurisdiction is wider.
Fundamental Rights are contained in **Articles 12 to 35** of **Part III** of the Indian Constitution.
Part III is rightly termed the **Magna Carta of India** due to its expansive guarantees.
Certain rights are exclusively for citizens: **Articles 15, 16, 19, 29, and 30**.
Rights like **Articles 14, 20, 21, 21A, 22, 23, 24, 25, 26, 27, and 28** apply to both citizens and foreigners.
Fundamental Rights are **justiciable**, allowing direct approach to the Supreme Court under **Article 32**.
Supreme Court issues writs under **Article 32** and High Courts under **Article 226**.
Rights under **Articles 20 and 21** remain operational even during a **National Emergency**.
Fundamental Duties were incorporated into **Part IV-A**, **Article 51A** via the **42nd Amendment, 1976**.
Fundamental Duties were added upon the recommendation of the **Swaran Singh Committee**.
There are currently **11 Fundamental Duties**, the last one added via the **86th Amendment, 2002**.

upscNotes.content: UPSSSC PET frequently asks exact article numbers, matching lists, and amendment years (especially 42nd and 86th). Memorize the exact article ranges for each category of Fundamental Rights.

Questions often trick students by stating that Fundamental Duties are legally enforceable. Remember: Duties are non-justiciable; courts cannot punish citizens directly for breaching a duty unless backed by ordinary law.
Focus heavily on landmark judgments like Kesavananda Bharati (1973), Maneka Gandhi (1978), and Puttaswamy (2017) as UPSSSC has increased case-law based questions in recent PET cycles.
Do not confuse Article 32 (Supreme Court writ jurisdiction) with Article 226 (High Court writ jurisdiction). High Court's jurisdiction is broader in scope regarding fundamental rights.

keyTakeaways: Fundamental Rights are enshrined in Part III (Articles 12-35) and borrowed from the USA.
Right to Property was removed from Part III by the 44th Amendment Act, 1978 and placed under Article 300A.
Article 32 is termed the 'Heart and Soul of the Constitution' by Dr. B.R. Ambedkar.
Fundamental Duties are enshrined in Part IV-A (Article 51A), borrowed from the USSR, and added by the 42nd Amendment, 1976.
There are 11 Fundamental Duties in total, with the 11th added by the 86th Amendment, 2002.
Articles 20 and 21 cannot be suspended even during a National Emergency.
Five types of writs are issued under Article 32 and Article 226: Habeas Corpus, Mandamus, Prohibition, Certiorari, and Quo-Warranto.
